newsitem.title: UK: BMW has eyes on Rolls-Royce says parent.
newsitem.headline: BMW has eyes on Rolls-Royce says parent.

text.p: Germany's Bayerische Motoren Werke AG (BMW) has had its eye on British car maker Rolls-Royce but knows a takeover bid would be rejected, the head of the British firm's parent Vickers Plc said on Wednesday.

Vickers chief executive Sir Colin Chandler said that BMW has not made a formal offer but he suspected BMW would like to do more than make engines for the British manufacturer. BMW was recruited two years ago to take over Rolls' engine requirements.
"I think BMW are interested," Chandler told Reuters. "I would not deny that at all and neither would they but the point is we are not selling."
Chandler said he believed Rolls-Royce could now survive as an independent carmaker having made a heavy invesment in modernising the business in the last five years.

"We spent a lot of money in the business in 1991/92 in both trading losses and in restructuring it. Our shareholders want to get that back and that's our job, to drive it for shareholder value which I think we are doing," he said.
Vickers earlier reported an 11 percent rise in group profits last year, to 83.3 million pounds before tax.

But operating profits from the automotive division, which includes Rolls-Royce Motor Cars and the Cosworth high performance engines specialist, fell 10 percent to 37.6 million pounds on a four percent rise in sales to 418.5 million pounds.
Roll-Royce increased sales by 12 percent to 1,744 cars last year but Chandler said margins were slightly down because of a "less rich mix" in sales and new investment on research and development.

He said the company aimed to increase profitability by concentrating on selling more bespoke versions of its cars but overall margins were likely to be "fairly steady" this year because of further development spending.
A new car would be ready for launch some time within the next three years, but the company was not ready to announce a date yet because it could effect sales of the current range, he said.
In contrast, operating profits at Vickers' Defence division rose 2.1 million pounds to 18 million pounds in 1996, on sales down 8.5 million pounds at 345.2 million.
But Chandler said the division continued to keep a lid on potential profits from its contract to supply 386 Challenger 2 tanks to the British Army until acceptance trials are completed.
Production is now running at a rate of about 100 tanks a year, with the tanks going into storage for the British Army pending delivery to regiments, which is expected after April 1998.
Vickers hit problems with the turret system but the latest field trials in southern England were going well, Chandler said, and he expected final trials to be completed in October this year.
Now Vickers needed to secure further sales to sustain production after the last British Army tanks are delviered in the year 2000.

Chandler told Reuters he was hopeful that existing customer Oman might confirm a follow-on order for 18 more Challengers later this year. Further ahead it is also competing with U.S. and French rivals to win orders from Saudi Arabia and Qatar, but these are not expected to be decided before 1998.

Mewanwhile, operating profits at Vickers third biggest division, Propulsion Technology, jumped by 6.9 million pounds last year to 24 million on sales up 22.7 percent at 292.4 million, boosted by aerospace components and its Kamewa Group marine propulsion business, which makes waterjets for high speed ferries.

Sales at the ailing medical equipment division fell 4.4 million pounds to 118.5 million pounds but operating profits made operating profits picked up slightly, to 1.6 million pounds from 900,000 in 1995 but further work needed to be done, Chandler said.
"We have clearly got a turnaround job going on there," he said.
